name: Colin Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a sheet-metal stamping press crew making appliance panels. I check the first panel after a die change and stop the press when a guard or edge looks wrong. My two-year technical diploma and years of careful setups put me among the strongest operators, and the lead wage is higher than most plants pay.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mara works at the public library, and our two school-age children live with us under a mortgage. We have roughly ten months saved and plenty of similar metal shops nearby. I have never used AI tools; I would rather check a drawing and ask a fitter, and I take paid-time complaints to our union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the stamping crew that office AI can file its own reports if it wants. A press still needs a sound die and a person who stops it when the guard misbehaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead wage is good, and we have about ten months of bills saved. Mara works at the public library and our two children are still at school; the mortgage is real, but several other metal shops are within reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the press crew on measured setup time and take our paid-minute records to the union pay meeting. From each full wage month I would add fresh money to the emergency account after bills, as we have done for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about my own work in this picture. I would still argue over unpaid setup minutes, because those minutes belong to someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you stop a press?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A guard that does not latch or a fresh panel with a torn edge. I isolate the machine and call the fitter before another sheet goes through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never. I hold a technical diploma and can read a die drawing, but I would rather ask the fitter than trust a chatbot.

say: I would ask for **sound press guards** before faster output.
I would bring **paid setup minutes** to union pay talks.
think: My **lead wage** and ten months saved protect the household.
Several **nearby metal shops** give me choices if ordinary orders slow.
do: Keep **press setup checks** and stop unsafe runs.
Add fresh **full-month wages** to emergency savings after bills.
feel: **Calm** about own work, still firm about paid time.
S0.quote: I would still argue over unpaid setup minutes, because those minutes belong to someone.
fieldNote: Colin’s **strong reserve** supports genuine calm about household money without muting his union concerns.
His saving is a **fresh wage transfer**, while press safety remains a daily concern.

steps.text: Keep press setup checks and stop unsafe runs
Bring paid setup records to union meeting
Add fresh full-month wages to emergency savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that AI can change purchasing and scheduling quickly, while robot press handling needs slower, guarded testing. Management should bargain over paid transfer places before it removes a helper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The camera might check panels and a loader might clear the stack, leaving fewer hands on the press. I expect my lead position to hold for now, but I would want the younger operators to get first shot at paid training rather than a quiet cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring roster and reject records to the union and ask for posted transfer openings. I would keep my current press shift, and if a co-worker loses hours, I would help them compare posted local metal jobs at wages after travel that cover their own bills; I would request a safe paid demonstration of the loader for our crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy for the team, though my own wage looks secure. An empty place on the rota is still a person missing at the break table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you operate the loader?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for an offered paid guarded practice place with the press isolated and a qualified fitter present. I would not claim I learned the controls from watching a demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask management to publish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which helper hours leave, the pay band for each transfer post and who gets to apply. I would take that list back to the branch.

say: I would demand **posted transfers** before helper hours disappear.
I would keep **guarded physical tests** separate from office scheduling.
think: A camera and loader could remove **helper hours**.
My own **lead wage** appears secure now, but the crew needs paid options.
do: Bring **rosters and rejects** to the union branch.
Keep **current press shift** and request a safe paid loader demonstration.
Help displaced **co-workers compare** posted adequate local metal jobs.
feel: **Uneasy** for the crew while own pay remains secure.
S1.quote: An empty place on the rota is still a person missing at the break table.
fieldNote: He seeks **collective transfer terms** before an actual helper cut.
His loader discussion is a **request for demonstration**, with no new controls learnt or offered practice place yet.

steps.text: Bring press rosters and rejects to union branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the branch that thinking AGI might arrive by 2028, but capable robots that handle dies and sheets come around 2031. The office may change first; our physical press work has a later date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of the press crew, including my lead hours, to be cut once robots safely change dies. Ten months saved will not replace my higher wage for years, and Mara’s library salary cannot carry the mortgage alone; I would lie awake over what the children lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the planned home extension and ask management for written staffing dates. If my shifts end, I would apply for posted reachable metal or safety roles only where net pay after travel covers our household bills; if no adequate post appears, I would ask the lender about a temporary payment plan and the union to press for wage protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by a likely large wage loss. I can organize a meeting, but I cannot make a posted vacancy stay open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not from a forecast. I would check mortgage terms and real job offers first, and protect the children’s school routine as long as the money allows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend savings on retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if an actual funded place and a posted job at enough net pay exist. I would keep a mortgage buffer rather than buy an uncertain certificate.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 press robots.
I would demand **written staffing dates** before physical cuts.
think: I expect **most press hours** and my lead wage to go.
Ten **months saved** and Mara’s pay cannot cover the house indefinitely.
do: Stop **extension plans** and request staffing dates.
Apply after **lost shifts** only for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work.
Ask **lender and union** about temporary protection if no adequate job appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless family worry.
S2.quote: I can organize a meeting, but I cannot make a posted vacancy stay open.
fieldNote: His **high wage** makes the expected replacement loss material despite a strong reserve.
Employment and mortgage relief remain **conditional** on actual cuts, posted local jobs, net pay after travel and lender approval.

steps.text: Stop extension plan and request written staffing dates
Apply after lost shifts for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work
Ask lender for temporary terms if no adequate job appears
Ask union to press for wage protection after job cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union that thinking AGI in 2031 and capable press robots around 2034 leave five years for real safety qualifications. A paid certificate is useful only if somebody posts the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight I will still need a wage for the mortgage and children. I know press guards and stopped-machine rules well, but I do not have a recognised safety assessor qualification or a promise of a local post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the press shift and put fresh full-month wages against mortgage principal. If the employer offers a funded safety-assessor course on paid time with an actual supervised place, and a posted reachable assessor role pays our bills after travel, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; otherwise I would look at posted local lead-operator work if my hours are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the line but able to test a real alternative. A course without a posted wage is a way to spend time, not a way to pay a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the safety course include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified assessor would isolate a press and let me check the guard and record the result. I would not sign a safety sheet after only watching a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a lower posted wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the take-home amount after travel still covers our household bills. Our savings buy time to compare, not a reason to accept a permanent shortfall.

say: I would seek **paid safety qualifications** before 2034 robots reach the sheet-metal press crew.
I would ask for **posted assessor wages** first.
think: The **mortgage wage** remains necessary at forty-eight.
My press skill needs a **recognised assessor place** to become another paid job.
do: Keep **press shifts** and pay extra mortgage from new wages.
Enrol in **funded paid safety training** only with supervised place and adequate posted job.
Apply after **qualification** for the reachable assessor role.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to compare actual jobs.
S3.quote: A course without a posted wage is a way to spend time, not a way to pay a mortgage.
fieldNote: He uses **existing press knowledge** as a possible bridge only after a recognised, funded qualification.
Training needs an **offered paid supervised place**; the later job requires local posting and bill-covering net wages.

steps.text: Pay extra mortgage principal from fresh full-month wages
Enrol if funded paid supervised assessor place and adequate posted job exist
Apply after qualification for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay assessor role
Search posted lead jobs after cuts if no course place opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the branch that thinking AGI in 2036 and capable press robots around 2039 leave time to negotiate paid places for the crew. We should put the transfer list in writing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty-three when thinking systems arrive and fifty-six when robots may handle the dies. The children will be adults, but neither the mortgage nor Mara’s library job comes with a promise for 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep leading the press line and add a fresh amount from regular wages to savings. If I am offered a funded paid safety course with supervised stopped-press practice and a posted reachable bill-covering net-pay role, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; in the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would compare real rosters and apply after sustained cuts only for safe adequate local work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about the distant machines while our present pay and savings are sound. I want the younger crew to have a signed training place, not a farewell cake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for pension and mortgage figures before deciding anything. If the numbers still need my wage, I will keep safe paid work and look at posted jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the written transfer list show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Names of the jobs, pay bands, paid training days and who can apply. I would bring it to the next branch meeting.

say: I would demand a **written transfer list** before 2039 robots.
I would keep **2036 systems** distinct from later press work.
think: Our **mortgage and library income** may change over thirteen years.
A long runway lets us **negotiate paid places** while wages still come in.
do: Keep **2026 press shifts** and save fresh regular wages.
Enrol in **funded paid safety training** only with offered practice and adequate posted role.
Apply after **post-2036 cuts** only for posted reachable safe bill-covering work.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant robots while current finances are sound.
S4.quote: I want the younger crew to have a signed training place, not a farewell cake.
fieldNote: His **current 2026 work** is separate from conditional post-2036 employment.
Course enrolment and later job moves require **offered paid safe practice**, posted reachable work and net wages sufficient after travel.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable press robots around 2031 could remove most lead hours. Written staffing dates, funded paid safe training and posted reachable jobs with bill-covering net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whose time made the machine safe enough to run. Our crew should be named when the company counts its savings.

headlineQuote: Our crew should be named when the company counts its savings.
portrait: **Colin**, 43, leads a sheet-metal stamping crew with a two-year technical diploma and strong safety judgement.
His **library-worker partner**, two school-age children, mortgage, higher operator pay, ten-month reserve and nearby metal shops give options.
He has **never used AI** and works through his union for paid time, guarded practice and written transfers.
Fast robots threaten **lead hours**; longer warning permits funded safety training and applications to actual posted work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before capable press robots threaten most of his lead wage around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered funded safe training and reachable posted roles at bill-covering net pay would help.
